messages.content:
Hi! Great questions.

Unfortunately, we couldn't include our code for exporting scene data out of 3ds Max in this repository. So you need to write your own exporter, but it's pretty easy. Your exporter just needs to generate data in the format that the rest of our pipeline is expecting. Have a look here and here for some example code.

When we're exporting our scene data out of 3ds Max, we must export information about each camera in the scene. The purpose of my_dataset/my_scene_N/_asset_export/metadata_cameras_asset_export.csv is to declare all the cameras that we export. We need to create this file manually in our exporter. Suppose we export three cameras from 3ds Max. At export time, we must give each of these cameras a unique name. For this example, let's suppose we decide to name the cameras cam_my_camera_00, cam_my_camera_01, cam_my_camera_02. The contents of metadata_cameras_asset_export.csv should be as follows:

camera_name
cam_my_camera_00
cam_my_camera_01
cam_my_camera_02


For each of these cameras, we must create a corresponding CSV file in the my_dataset/my_scene_N/_asset_export directory. The CSV file must have the same name as the camera, e.g., cam_my_camera_00.csv, cam_my_camera_01.csv, cam_my_camera_02.csv. We need to create each of these files manually in our exporter.

This exported camera data is eventually consumed here.

Note that my_dataset/my_scene_N/_asset_export/metadata_cameras_asset_export.csv isn't exactly the same as my_dataset/my_scene_N/_detail/metadata_cameras.csv. In metadata_cameras_asset_export.csv the cameras can have any names, but in metadata_cameras.csv they get renamed to standard names that are used throughout the rest of our pipeline cam_00, cam_01, cam_02.

Can you ask your FOV question in a separate thread, so it'll be easier for other folks to find it? I'll answer in the new thread.

messages.content:
Hi! Great question. NaN values can and do occur in the Hypersim images when there is no scene geometry at that pixel. In the case of {ai_035_001, cam_00, frame.0001}, we see that there are indeed some "empty" pixels, i.e., pixels that don't observe any scene geometry. Here are some preview images from this frame.

frame.0001.tonemap.jpg

frame.0001.depth_meters.png

White values in the frame.0001.depth_meters.png preview image indicates empty pixels, and we expect to have NaN values in these pixels in our HDF5 files. The exact pixel coordinate you're referring to appears to correspond to the top-right pixel of the right-most window.

In summary, you're seeing a NaN value because there is no geometry at that pixel, and therefore the pixel's world-space position is undefined.

messages.content:
We also came across this issue when we tried to use the Evermotion data set in a multi view geometry application.
For example in volume 44, scene 2 some pixel blobs in the depth image are not defined:


Quite many scenes have small portions that have undefined geometry information. When trying to backproject all pixels p of one frame into its own camera plane using the pixel world position r_WP, camera intrinsics K, and camera pose T_CW, i.e.,

p_projected = K * T_CW * r_WP(p_original)


we'd expect p_projected == p_original. The histogram below shows the maximum reprojection error for every frame. We suspect that any image that has a maximum reprojection error greater than 100 pixel contains missing geometry information.

We did not cross-compare whether huge reprojection errors are always caused by undefined geometry information.
However, we made the frame-to-itself reprojection results available.
Thus users can possibly remove frames or mask frame patches where the geometry information is problematic.

messages.content:
So why do we need that (admittedly confusing) chunk of code that you referred to in your original question?

The need for this code arises because we want to support rendering with very general lens distortion effects. More specifically, we want users to be able to specify the exact ray they want to cast at every pixel, because then we can render data for all kinds of custom cameras. Do you have a custom camera with really weird fisheye lens distortion? No problem. Just provide modify_vrscene_add_camera.py with a dense array of rays in camera space that match your camera model, and we'll make sure that our final rendered images match your camera model. We think that requiring users to specify a dense array of rays in camera space is the cleanest way to specify lens distortion effects. Otherwise we'd need to decide in advance on some kind of compact parameterization (e.g., the polynomial distortion model used in OpenCV), and that parameterization might not be a good fit for your specific camera.

Under the hood, V-Ray supports user-specified per-pixel lens distortion effects, but it does so in a somewhat indirect way. Instead of specifying a dense array of rays in camera space, V-Ray requires you to specify an FOV and a dense array of UV-values, where each UV-coordinate is in the range [-1,1], and each UV-value corresponds to a point on the undistorted 2D image plane (see the V-Ray documentation for details). Note that the FOV is required to map a particular UV-value to a particular ray in camera space.

There is a mismatch between the interface we want to provide to our users (specifying a dense array of rays in camera space), and the interface that our renderer supports (specifying an FOV and a dense array of UV-values). Fortunately, it is easy to convert back and forth from one representation to the other. When you provide us with an array of camera rays, we simply find the smallest undistorted camera frustum that will accomodate all of your rays (in other words, we solve for the smallest possible FOV), and then express your rays in terms of UV-values that are correct for that camera frustum.

When expressing your rays in terms of UV-values, there is no harm in choosing a camera frustum that is slightly larger than necessary, and we do this intentionally to avoid rounding errors. For example, suppose we determine that the smallest possible FOV that will accomodate all of your rays is fov_x = 1.23456789, and we compute UV-values that are correct for this exact FOV. As our pipeline loads, transforms, and saves various intermediate copies of the scene, the V-Ray Python SDK may only save our original value of fov_x = 1.23456789 as fov_x = 1.23. In this case, the UV-values that we computed previously will be slightly incorrect. To avoid this problem, we apply some of our own numerical padding when we're solving for the appropriate FOV (e.g., we will intentionally set fov_x = 1.24), so that it can be loaded and saved without any loss of precision by the V-Ray Python SDK, and our UV-values will be exactly correct.

We have determined empirically (using our own bare-bones ray tracer that we implemented from scratch as ground truth), that this approach leads to V-Ray renderings that more faithfully match your user-specified lens distortion. In other words, if you don't apply this numerical padding carefully, then you'll think that you're rendering with a particular lens distortion model, but V-Ray will actually be rendering with a slightly different lens distortion model.

There is a mismatch between the interface we want to provide to our users (specifying a dense array of rays in camera space), and the interface that our renderer supports (specifying an FOV and a dense array of UV-values). Fortunately, it is easy to convert back and forth from one representation to the other. When you provide us with an array of camera rays, we simply find the smallest undistorted camera frustum that will accomodate all of your rays (in other words, we solve for the smallest possible FOV), and then express your rays in terms of UV-values that are correct for that camera frustum.

When expressing your rays in terms of UV-values, there is no harm in choosing a camera frustum that is slightly larger than necessary, and we do this intentionally to avoid rounding errors. For example, suppose we determine that the smallest possible FOV that will accomodate all of your rays is fov_x = 1.23456789, and we compute UV-values that are correct for this exact FOV. As our pipeline loads, transforms, and saves various intermediate copies of the scene, the V-Ray Python SDK may only save our original value of fov_x = 1.23456789 as fov_x = 1.23. In this case, the UV-values that we computed previously will be slightly incorrect. To avoid this problem, we apply some of our own numerical padding when we're solving for the appropriate FOV (e.g., we will intentionally set fov_x = 1.24), so that it can be loaded and saved without any loss of precision by the V-Ray Python SDK, and our UV-values will be exactly correct.

We have determined empirically (using our own bare-bones ray tracer that we implemented from scratch as ground truth), that this approach leads to V-Ray renderings that more faithfully match your user-specified lens distortion. In other words, if you don't apply this numerical padding carefully, then you'll think that you're rendering with a particular lens distortion model, but V-Ray will actually be rendering with a slightly different lens distortion model.

The need for this code arises because we want to support rendering with very general lens distortion effects. More specifically, we want users to be able to specify the exact ray they want to cast at every pixel, because then we can render data for all kinds of custom cameras. Just provide modify_vrscene_add_camera.py with a dense array of rays in camera space that match your camera model, and we'll make sure that our final rendered images match your camera model. Otherwise we'd need to decide in advance on some kind of compact parameterization (e.g., the polynomial distortion model used in OpenCV), and that parameterization might not be a good fit for your specific camera.

Hi! Great question.

All of the native scene content for Hypersim comes in the form of 3ds Max files, so you have no choice but to interact with 3ds Max at least once per scene. In our pipeline, we choose to interact with 3ds Max as briefly as possible, by exporting all the data into cross-platform assets as early as possible, and working with the cross-platform assets throughout the rest of our pipeline.

messages.content:
Hi! Great questions.

First, the scene you showed in your figure (ai_001_003) really is that shade of blue. You can see it in the thumbnails on the original artist's website:

https://evermotion.org/shop/show_product/archinteriors-vol-1/37

These artist thumbnails are not rendered by our pipeline, and therefore offer an independent sanity check for what our rendered images should look like. We do not expect our rendered images to match these artist thumbnails exactly, because the artist renderings use a different tone-mapping algorithm, and sometimes also have manual post-processing applied to them. In contrast, we intentionally avoid manual post-processing in our pipeline, and we use a simple tone-mapping algorithm to maximize the consistency of our output. Despite these minor differences, the artist thumbnails should be visually similar to our rendered images (i.e., you'd be able to tell by visual inspection if we accidentally swapped color channels).

Second, our HDF5 data is the most raw possible data available from the renderer. It has no normalization or tone mapping or gamma correction or other non-linear color transformations applied to it. In other words, the value at each pixel is proportional to outbound radiance. There is a huge range of radiance values in a typical real-world indoor scene, and therefore we expect a huge range of radiance values in our HDF5 data. It is also expected that different parts of the same scene have different ranges of radiance values. For example, a really bright light might be visible in one part of the scene, but not another, and this could lead to one image having a wider range of radiance values than another.

I agree that working with raw rendered data comes with additional challenges. But it also has distinct advantages. In particular, our data adheres to the equation final_image == diffuse_reflectance * diffuse_illumination + non_diffuse_residual, which is a useful property in inverse rendering applications, and this property would not hold if we applied non-linear color transformations to our rendered data. Therefore, we leave it up to the user to apply whatever tone-mapping operations (if any) that makes the most sense in their application. If you don't like the wide range of radiance values in our HDF5 data, can you just apply our tone-mapping code in your application?

messages.content: @rikba The dynamic range in raw Hypersim images is huge, just like dynamic range of real images from a real camera. It is not useful to map the min and max values in each image linearly to the range [0,1], which is what cv2.normalize(...) is doing. Instead, you need to apply a tone-mapping algorithm to compress the huge dynamic range in these images in a meaningful way.

messages.content:
Great question! It is always a good idea to experiment with the mesh data and camera data, to make sure you're interpreting it all correctly.

Let's assume you obtained your own copy of the source assets, exported an OBJ file for a particular scene, and then ran our code/python/tools/generate_mesh_from_obj.py code for that scene. In this case, you will have the following files in the _detail/mesh folder for that scene:

mesh_vertices.hdf5 contains a Vx3 array of vertex positions for the entire scene
mesh_faces_vi.hdf5 contains an Fx3 array of faces for the entire scene; this array stores integer IDs that refer to the values in the mesh_vertices array
If mesh_faces_vi[i] == [a b c], it means that the ith face in the scene is a triangle with vertices (v0, v1, v2) == (mesh_vertices[a], mesh_vertices[b], mesh_vertices[c])
mesh_faces_oi.hdf5 contains an Fx1 array with the "object ID" of each face; note that these "object IDs" are the most fine-grained segmentation available in our data, and are more fine-grained than our semantic instance IDs; in other words, each "semantic instance" in our data is composed of several "object IDs"
mesh_objects_sii.hdf5 contains a Bx1 array with the semantic instance ID of each object ID
mesh_objects_si.hdf5 contains a Bx1 array with the NYU40 semantic label for each object ID

To understand how to project this mesh data onto our pre-rendered images, here are some steps that will be helpful, in increasing order of difficulty:

Load the mesh data into your own interactive viewer to make sure you understand the mesh format. For this step, don't worry about aligning the mesh data to any particular camera pose. I implement something like this in code/python/tools/visualize_mesh.py that you can use as a reference. In my code, I use mayavi for visualizing the mesh, but any interactive viewer library should work.

Select a single semantic instance from the mesh data and visualize only that instance. Manually choose an instance that is visible in a pre-rendered image, get the semantic instance ID from the segmentation ground truth image, and use the semantic instance ID to select the appropriate vertices and faces from the mesh data. In my code (code/python/tools/visualize_mesh.py), I render each semantic instance separately in a different color, so there is already the necessary logic in this file to select a single semantic instance from the mesh data.

Once you're familiar with the mesh format, try projecting the mesh vertices for a single instance onto one of our pre-rendered images. The projected vertices should align pixel-perfectly with the pre-rendered image. This step will require using the camera ground truth data for that particular image. I implement something like this in code/python/tools/scene_generate_images_bounding_box.py that you can use as a reference. In my code, I project each 3D corner of the semantic instance's bounding box (8 corners in total), but you could just as easily project mesh vertices instead of bounding box corners. In my code, there is a bit of extra logic to render lines rather than points, and to render everything in the correct depth order. You can ignore all of this additional logic, since the goal here is simply to project a collection of points in a way that aligns with a pre-rendered image (i.e., you don't need to worry about rendering lines, and you don't need to worry about rendering things in the correct depth order). At this point, you have re-implemented the complete geometric transformation pipeline in Hypersim.

Give these steps a try, and post here if you run into any problems

messages.content:
Hi! All of our camera poses are given in the ground truth data. See our README for a detailed description of precisely how they're stored, and precisely how to interpret the stored values.

Given the camera rotation matrix for a particular image, you can find the "roll angle" you're looking for with a bit of linear algebra. Roughly speaking, you want to rotate the camera rotation matrix about its "forward" direction, such that its "right" direction lies in the horizontal plane. Stating this problem more precisely, you want to find a rotation matrix R, parameterized by a roll angle theta, such that the following condition holds:

# rotate our camera and return the camera's new right vector
rotated_camera_right_vector = get_right_vector(R(theta)*original_camera_rotation_matrix))

# compute the right vector that lies in the horizontal plane
original_camera_forward_vector = get_forward_vector(original_camera_rotation_matrix)
rotated_camera_right_vector_horizontal = cross(original_camera_forward_vector, world_space_gravity_vector)

# we want our right vector after rotation to lie in the horizontal plane
assert rotated_camera_right_vector == rotated_camera_right_vector_horizontal


Once you have found theta, you can either rotate our pre-rendered images by theta in image-space, or you can modify our camera poses and re-render images from scratch. In both cases, you'll end up with "upright" images.

messages.content:
That quote is from the "3D bounding boxes" section of the documentation, which describes our conventions for the 3D bounding boxes we compute around each semantic instance. This is the wrong place to look. The "coordinate conventions" section of the documentation describes our camera conventions. This is the right place to look.

We store orientations as 3x3 rotation matrices that map points to world-space from object-space, assuming that points are stored as [x,y,z] column vectors. Our convention for storing camera orientations is that the camera's positive x-axis points right, the positive y-axis points up, and the positive z-axis points away from where the camera is looking.

You should make sure you're adhering to our camera conventions. For our scenes, I believe the world-space vector that points from the ground to the sky is [0 0 1]. You can use this vector for the gravity vector, or [0 0 -1], as long as you're consistent. Depending on which convention you choose for the gravity vector, you will need to swap the order of the arguments to the cross product operator. If you do the cross product backwards, you'll end up computing the roll angle that rotates the image to be exactly upside down, instead of exactly upright.

messages.content:
Hi! Great questions. Here is a quick high-level description of each image in the scene_cam_XX_final_preview folder.

color is the color image produced the renderer without tonemapping and without gamma correction.
diff measures how well the diffuse_reflectance, diffuse_illumination, and residual images reconstruct the color image; it is calculated as diff = abs(color - (diffuse_reflectance*diffuse_illumination + residual)).
diffuse_illumination is described in the paper.
diffuse_reflectance is described in the paper.
gamma is the color image without tonemapping and with gamma correction.
lambertian is the reconstructed color image excluding all non-diffuse energy; it is calculated as lambertian = diffuse_reflectance*diffuse_illumination
non_lambertian is the reconstructed color image including all non-diffuse energy; this image should closely match the color image. it is calculated as non_lambertian = diffuse_reflectance*diffuse_illumination + residual.
residual is described in the paper.
tonemap is the color image with tonemapping and with gamma correction.

You can see for yourself how each of these preview images is calculated in code/python/tools/generate_hdf5_from_vrimg.py and code/python/tools/scene_generate_images_tonemap.py.

x = u / fx * depth
y = v / fy * depth 
z = - depth

Here (u, v) is the pixel coordinate in ndc space with +u pointing right and +v pointing up (here in your code), (fx, fy) are the camera's focal length (e.g. here in your code)

messages.content:
Hi Georgia! At first glance, your reasoning looks correct, and you are looking at all the right places in the code where these coordinate conventions are established and implemented. However, I'm arriving at a slightly different expression for xyz_cam1. I'm sure there will be other things to debug as we're getting on the same page with our coordinate conventions, but can you double check my reasoning and see if my slightly different expression for xyz_cam1 works for you? 

# equation 1: I'm assuming that the "camera orientation" matrix is R0, and the "camera position" vector is T0

xyz_world0 = (R0 * xyz_cam0) + T0



(See here for an example of where equation 1 is implemented in our code)

# equation 2: same as above, but for xyz_world1, re-arranged in terms of xyz_cam1

xyz_world1 = (R1 * xyz_cam1) + T1

xyz_world1 - T1 = R1 * xyz_cam1

R1.T * (xyz_world1 - T1) = xyz_cam1



# let xyz_world0 == xyz_world1, substitute equation 1 into equation 2, collect terms

# note that we arrive at a final expression for xyz_cam1 that is slightly different from the one in your initial post

xyz_cam1 = R1.T * (((R0 * xyz_cam0) + T0) - T1)

xyz_cam1 = R1.T * ((R0 * xyz_cam0) + T0) - R1.T * T1

xyz_cam1 = R1.T * (R0 * xyz_cam0) + R1.T * T0 - R1.T * T1

xyz_cam1 = R1.T * (R0 * xyz_cam0) + R1.T * (T0 - T1)

Yay! I'm glad you figured this out  Thank you for highlighting these ambiguities in our documentation. I'll try my best to respond point-by-point to your posts for anyone else reading this, and I'll leave this issue open until I get a chance to clarify the documentation.

depth_meters is the Euclidean distance in meters to the optical center of the camera. It should really be called distance_from_camera_meters. I apologize for the unclear naming convention  Regardless, this is not the same as the negative z-coordinate in camera space. See #9 for a handy code snippet (contributed by @sniklaus) that converts these Euclidean distance values into planar depth values.
You're using the correct rotation and translation matrices. camera_keyframe_orientations stores the R matrices directly, and camera_keyframe_positions stores the T vectors directly. Since we agree on equations 1 and 2 in my post above, I believe you are converting to world-space from camera-space correctly.
Your xyz_world values should exactly match the values stored in our frame.IIII.position.hdf5 images, assuming you're working in asset units, i.e., not meters.
For each scene, the _detail/metadata_scene.csv file defines a meters_per_asset_unit scale factor that can be used to convert between asset units and meters.

messages.content:
I don't know exactly what "homography warping" is, and I don't know what you mean when you're saying you'd like to "warp frame0 to frame1". Anyway, I'm interpreting your question as follows. Most of the time, frame 0 and frame 1 will observe many of the same points, but they will be at different pixel locations (e.g., a coffee mug might be in the corner of frame 0 but closer to the center of frame 1). So, for all the points that are visible in frame 0, you would like to compute their pixel locations in frame 1.

The easiest way is to start with frame.0000.position.hdf5, because this file contains the world-space positions for each pixel in frame 0.
You need to project these world-space points into the camera-space for frame 1, and then you need to project these camera-space points into the screen-space for frame 1 to compute their final pixel locations. See our scene_generate_images_bounding_box.py for an end-to-end code example. In this example, we project the corners of a 3D bounding box from world-space to screen-space using the camera information stored in the Hypersim data.
To verify your understanding, you can also try this entire exercise starting with frame.0000.depth_meters.hdf5. This file contains distance values in meters, not world-space positions, and therefore requires a couple of extra conversion steps. I recommend getting things working the easy way first, and then posting a new question if you have questions about working with frame.0000.depth_meters.hdf5.

See our scene_generate_images_bounding_box.py for an end-to-end code example. In this example, we project the corners of a 3D bounding box from world-space to screen-space using the camera information stored in the Hypersim data.
  • To verify your understanding, you can also try this entire exercise starting with frame.0000.depth_meters.hdf5. This file contains distance values in meters, not world-space positions, and therefore requires a couple of extra conversion steps. I recommend getting things working the easy way first, and then posting a new question if you have questions about working with frame.0000.depth_meters.hdf5.

messages.content:
Hi! Great question.

A label value of -1 indicates not labeled, a label value of 0 should never occur in our HDF5 images, and a label value in the range 1-40 (inclusive) maps to the semantic classes defined here.

The NYU40 label set has an interesting history. The original NYUv2 dataset (Silberman et al. 2012) defines a label set consisting of 894 labels, and the NYU40 label set was defined later (Gupta et al. 2013). Gupta's code expects the mapping from NYU894 labels to NYU40 labels to be stored in a classMapping40 Matlab variable, but this variable isn't defined anywhere in his code. Fortunately, I have tracked down a copy of the original classMapping40 variable, and it defines values in the range 1-40 (inclusive), not in the range 0-39 inclusive. This indexing convention makes sense, because the mapping was originally designed to be used in Matlab code. Anyway, as far as I can tell, the "official" representation of NYU40 labels is for them to be in the range 1-40 (inclusive), and this is the convention we adopt in Hypersim

Hi! The images you care about are stored directly in the ZIP files that you can download. For example:

ai_001_001/images/scene_cam_XX_final_hdf5/frame.0000.color.hdf5 # color image before any tonemapping has been applied

ai_001_001/images/scene_cam_XX_geometry_hdf5/frame.0000.semantic.hdf5 # semantic IDs using NYU40 labels



HDF5 files are multi-dimensional array files that are easy to read and write from C++ and Python. See our usage of the h5py module throughout the code for examples on how to load these files into NumPy arrays. It is only necessary to run dataset_generate_images_semantic_segmentation.py if you have re-labeled the meshes or if you're doing your own rendering.

I hope that helps! Also, thank you for your contribution to the download script

HDF5 files are multi-dimensional array files that are easy to read and write from C++ and Python. See our usage of the h5py module throughout the code for examples on how to load these files into NumPy arrays. It is only necessary to run dataset_generate_images_semantic_segmentation.py if you have re-labeled the meshes or if you're doing your own rendering.

messages.content:
Ah I understand. Unfortunately, what you want to do is not possible without purchasing the assets, and parsing the V-Ray scene description file as I described above.

Alternatively, if anyone is reading this and wants to re-render their own images anyway, it is possible to output more fine-grained lighting and shading information than we do in Hypersim. In particular, it is possible to distinguish between specular, reflective, and refractive surfaces by configuring V-Ray to output the following render elements: VRaySpecular, VRayReflection, and VRayRefraction.

(However, I don't believe outputting these render elements would distinguish between a specular black object and a shiny metal object. In both cases, the non-diffuse energy would be contained in the VRaySpecular render element. To make such a fine-grained distinction, I believe it would be necessary to parse the materials in the scene description file.)
